title: Tepotinib Therapy for Advanced MET Exon 14 Skipping NSCLC With Non‐Dialysis End‐Stage Renal Disease: A Case Report
author: Susumu Yamazaki; Yoshiaki Nagai; Hitomi Watanabe; Yoshitaka Uchida; Takeshi Asato; Kyosuke Kasaoka; Konjo Cho; Makoto Nagata
text:
ABSTRACT
Tepotinib is an oral mesenchymal–epithelial transition factor (MET) tyrosine kinase inhibitor approved for advanced or metastatic MET exon 14 skipping non‐small cell lung cancer (NSCLC). While no dose adjustment is required in patients with mild‐to‐moderate renal impairment, evidence in those with severe renal dysfunction remains limited. We report a case of advanced MET exon 14 skipping NSCLC in a patient with end‐stage renal disease (ESRD) without dialysis who was successfully treated with tepotinib. During therapy, serum creatinine increased, whereas serum cystatin C remained stable, suggesting pseudo‐acute kidney injury due to inhibition of renal tubular transporters. Tepotinib was resumed at a reduced dose without further renal deterioration, resulting in a partial tumour response. This case highlights the feasibility of tepotinib therapy in carefully selected patients with ESRD and underscores the clinical utility of incorporating complementary renal biomarkers, cystatin C, for guiding treatment decisions and avoiding unnecessary treatment discontinuation.
Keywords: creatinine, cystatin C, end‐stage renal disease (ESRD), estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR), lung cancer, mesenchymal–epithelial transition factor (MET), MET exon 14 skipping, Tepotinib, tyrosine kinase inhibitor (TKI)
During tepotinib treatment, serum creatinine levels increased, whereas serum cystatin C remained stable. Chest computed tomography showed tumour shrinkage consistent with a partial response, which was maintained at 6 months.
1. Introduction
Renal dysfunction is a prevalent comorbidity in patients with lung cancer, affecting approximately 28%, and severe renal impairment develops in approximately 2%. The risk of developing lung cancer increases 1.0–1.5‐fold after kidney transplantation. Chronic kidney disease (CKD) and end‐stage renal disease (ESRD) requiring dialysis are associated with poor clinical outcomes in lung cancer due to limited therapeutic tolerance and competing morbidities. Mesenchymal–epithelial transition factor (MET) exon 14 skipping mutations occur in approximately 3%–4% of non‐small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) cases, primarily in older adults. Although this alteration is associated with a poor prognosis under standard therapy, it represents an actionable driver mutation and predicts responsiveness to MET‐targeted TKIs. Tepotinib, a highly selective oral MET inhibitor, received regulatory approval based on results from the VISION trial [1]. Its pharmacokinetics remain stable in patients with mild‐to‐moderate renal impairment (CLcr 30–89 mL/min), and dose adjustment is not necessary. However, patients with severe renal dysfunction (CLcr < 30 mL/min) were excluded from pivotal studies. Because tepotinib undergoes predominantly biliary elimination with limited renal clearance [2], severe renal impairment is unlikely to substantially affect its metabolism. Herein, we describe the first case of successful tepotinib therapy in a patient with ESRD without dialysis, with emphasis on the clinical use of cystatin C in the management of pseudo‐acute kidney injury (AKI).
2. Case Report
A 75‐year‐old man with no respiratory symptoms exhibited a nodular opacity in the right lower lung field on routine chest radiography (Figure 1A). He had a history of diabetic nephropathy with progressive renal dysfunction since the age of 63. Initial laboratory tests were consistent with ESRD, with a serum creatinine level of 5.00 mg/dL and an estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR), calculated using the MDRD equation, of < 10 mL/min/1.73 m2. Despite meeting ESRD criteria, dialysis was not initiated due to preserved diuresis and a stable clinical condition. Chest computed tomography (CT) showed a 36 × 22 mm solitary nodule located in segments 8 and 9 of the right lower lobe (Figure 1B). Transbronchial biopsy confirmed adenocarcinoma. Molecular analysis using a next‐generation sequencing panel (AmoyDx) identified a MET exon 14 skipping mutation. The PD‐L1(22C3) tumour proportion score was 5%. The clinical stage was cT2aN1M1a (stage IVA), and the Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group performance status was 0. Tepotinib was started at 500 mg once daily. At baseline, serum creatinine was 4.96 mg/dL, and cystatin C was 3.81 mg/L. On day 6 of treatment, serum creatinine increased to 6.66 mg/dL, while cystatin C remained stable at 3.71 mg/L. Despite the absence of symptoms, tepotinib was temporarily withheld as a precaution. x‐ray on day 9 revealed tumour shrinkage. Pseudo‐AKI caused by inhibition of renal tubular transporters such as multidrug and toxin extrusion protein 1 (MATE‐1) was suspected. Tepotinib was resumed at a reduced dose of 250 mg daily on day 10. Renal function was stable (serum creatinine 7.32 mg/dL on day 13), and the patient was discharged in stable condition on day 17. Subsequently, tepotinib was continued at 250 mg daily. On day 49, serum creatinine was 6.36 mg/dL, and CT indicated a partial response, with tumour size reduced to 28 × 12 mm (Figure 2). According to the Response Evaluation Criteria in Solid Tumours (RECIST), the target lesion showed a partial response, non‐target lesions showed non‐progressive disease, and no new lesions were observed. The overall response was therefore judged as a partial response. The only treatment‐related adverse event was grade 1 (Common Terminology Criteria for Adverse Events) peripheral edema. The patient remained clinically stable and active and well throughout therapy.
3. Discussion
To our knowledge, this is the first reported case of tepotinib use in a patient with advanced NSCLC and ESRD who was not receiving dialysis. Although the safety of tepotinib in patients with mild‐to‐moderate renal impairment is established, clinical data in ESRD remain sparse, primarily due to the exclusion of this population from pivotal clinical trials. Tepotinib has been shown to elevate serum creatinine by inhibiting renal tubular transporters such as MATE‐1, without affecting true glomerular filtration rate. This can result in pseudo‐AKI, wherein creatinine rises independently of renal injury [3, 4]. In the present case, cystatin C—a filtration marker not influenced by tubular secretion—remained stable, enabling distinction between pseudo‐AKI and true nephrotoxicity. This enabled safe continuation of therapy following dose adjustment, thereby avoiding unnecessary discontinuation of an effective treatment. The use of cystatin C as a complementary biomarker for renal function with nephrotoxic agents has been recognised, and it may be particularly valuable during TKI therapy in patients with impaired renal reserve. Routine cystatin C monitoring could facilitate risk stratification and more nuanced renal assessment, especially in high‐risk populations. Pharmacokinetic data further support the feasibility of tepotinib in ESRD. Approximately 85% of the drug is excreted in faeces, and 13.6% is eliminated renally [2]. A previous case report describing the use of tepotinib in a dialysis‐dependent patient also demonstrated safety and tolerability [5]. The current case extends these observations to patients with ESRD without dialysis.
In summary, tepotinib was safely and effectively used in a patient with advanced MET exon 14 skipping NSCLC and ESRD without dialysis. The case underscores the importance of tailoring renal monitoring approaches in patients with advanced kidney disease undergoing TKI therapy and highlights the role of cystatin C in guiding safe oncologic treatment in this setting.
